source_text: Cum vero praescribitur nemini sine Baptismo competere salutem, ex illa maxime pronuntiatione Domini, qui ait: Nisi natus ex aqua quis erit, non habet vitam, suboriuntur scrupulosi, imo temerarii retractatus quorumdam, quomodo ex ista praescriptione Apostolis salus competat, quos tinctos non invenimus in Domino, praeter Paulum. Imo cum Paulus solus ex illis Baptismum Christi induerit, aut praejudicatum esse de caeterorum periculo, qui careant aqua Christi, ut praescriptio salva sit, aut rescindi praescriptionem, si etiam non tinctis salus statuta est. Audivi, Domino teste, ejusmodi, ne quis me tam perditum existimet, ut ultro exagitem libidine styli, quae aliis scrupulum incutiant. Et nunc illis, ut potero, respondebo, qui negant Apostolos tinctos. Nam si humanum Joannis Baptismum inierant, et dominicum desiderabant quatenus unum Baptismum definierat ipse Dominus, dicens Petro perfundi nolenti: Qui semel lavit, non habet necesse rursum: quod utique non tincto non omnino dixisset: et haec est probatio exserta adversus illos, qui adimunt Apostolis etiam Joannis Baptismum, ut destruant aquae sacramentum. An credibile videri potest, in his personis viam tunc Domini praeparatam, id est Baptismum Joannis, quae ad viam Domini per totum orbem aperiendam destinabantur? Ipse Dominus, nullius poenitentiae debitor, tinctus est, peccatoribus non fuit necesse? Quid ergo? alii tincti non sunt? non tamen comites Christi, sed aemuli fidei, legis doctores et Pharisaei. Unde et suggeritur, cum adversantes Domino tingui noluerint, eos qui Dominum sequebantur, tinctos fuisse, nec cum aemulis suis sapuisse, maxime quando Dominus cui adhaerebant, testimonio Joannem extulisset, nemo, dicens, major inter natos foeminarum Joanne baptizatore. Alii plane satis coacte injiciunt tunc apostolos Baptismi vicem implesse cum in navicula fluctibus aspersi operti sunt; ipsum quoque Petrum per mare ingredientem satis mersum. Ut opinor autem, aliud aspergi vel intercipi violentia maris, aliud tingui disciplina religionis. Caeterum navicula illa figuram Ecclesiae praeferebat, quod in mari, id est saeculo, fluctibus, id est persecutionibus et tentationibus inquietatur Domino per patientiam velut dormiente, donec orationibus Sanctorum in ultimis suscitatus, compescat saeculum et tranquillitatem suis reddat. Nunc sive tincti quoquo modo fuerunt, sive illoti perseveraverunt, ut et illud dictum Domini, de uno lavacro sub Petri persona ad nos tantummodo spectet, de salute tamen Apostolorum satis temerarium est aestimare, quia illis vel primae allectionis, et exinde individuae familiaritatis praerogativa compendium Baptismi conferre posset. Cum illo, opinor, sequebantur illum, qui credenti cuique salutem pollicebatur: Fides tua te, aiebat, salvum fecit, et: Remittuntur tibi peccata, credenti utique, nec tamen tincto. Id si Apostolis defuit, nescio quorum fides: uno verbo Domini suscitatus teloneum dereliquit; patrem, et navem, et artem qua vitam sustentabat, deseruit; patris exequias despexit: summum illud Domini praeceptum: Qui patrem aut matrem mihi praetulerit, non est me dignus, ante perfecit quam audivit.
pass_a_gloss: But when it is prescribed that no one can attain salvation without Baptism, from that very pronouncement of the Lord, who says: Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life, there arise scrupulous, or rather reckless, objections of some, as to how from this prescription salvation can be granted to the Apostles, whom we do not find to have been baptized in the Lord, except for Paul. Indeed, since Paul alone of them put on the Baptism of Christ, either the judgment about the danger of the others, who lack the water of Christ, must be prejudged, so that the prescription may be saved, or the prescription must be rescinded, if salvation is also established for those who are not baptized. I have heard, with the Lord as witness, such things, lest anyone think me so lost as to voluntarily stir up with the lust of the pen what inspires scruple in others. And now I will respond, as I can, to those who deny that the Apostles were baptized. For if they had undergone human Baptism, that of John, and desired the Lord's, inasmuch as the Lord Himself had defined one Baptism, saying to Peter, who was unwilling to be washed: He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again, which He would not have said at all to one who was not baptized; and this is the evident proof against those who deny the Apostles even John's Baptism, so that they may destroy the sacrament of water. Can it be believed that, in the case of those persons, the way of the Lord was then being prepared, that is, the Baptism of John, who were destined to open the way of the Lord throughout the whole world? The Lord Himself, who owed no debt of repentance, was baptized; was it not necessary for sinners? What then? Were others not baptized? Not, however, the companions of Christ, but the rivals of faith, the teachers of the law, and the Pharisees. Whence it is also suggested that, when those who opposed the Lord were unwilling to be baptized, those who followed the Lord were baptized, and did not have a taste of their rivals, especially when the Lord, to whom they adhered, extolled John in testimony, saying: No one is greater among those born of women than John the Baptist. Others plainly force the idea that the Apostles then fulfilled the role of Baptism when they were sprinkled and covered by the waves in the boat; and that Peter also was sufficiently immersed when he walked into the sea. But, in my opinion, it is one thing to be sprinkled or intercepted by the violence of the sea, and another to be baptized by the discipline of religion. Moreover, that boat represented the figure of the Church, which is troubled in the sea, that is, the world, by waves, that is, persecutions and temptations, while the Lord is asleep, as it were, through patience, until, aroused by the prayers of the Saints in the last times, He restrains the world and gives tranquility to His own. Now, whether they were baptized in some way or remained unbaptized, and whether that saying of the Lord, about one washing, under the person of Peter, refers only to us, it is nevertheless too reckless to estimate the salvation of the Apostles, because for them the privilege of the first calling, and from then on of individual familiarity, could confer the compendium of Baptism. For they followed Him, who promised salvation to each believer: Your faith has saved you, He said, and: Your sins are forgiven, certainly to the believer, and not to the baptized. If this was lacking to the Apostles, I do not know of what faith they were; with one word of the Lord, the tax collector arose and left his post; he deserted his father, and his boat, and the skill by which he sustained his life; he despised his father's funeral: he fulfilled that greatest commandment of the Lord, He who prefers his father or mother to me is not worthy of me, before he heard it.

pass_b_english: When the rule is laid down that no one attains salvation without Baptism, based on the Lord's own pronouncement—"Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life" (John 3:5)—some people raise scrupulous, or rather reckless, objections: how can the Apostles qualify for salvation under that rule, since we do not find them baptized in the Lord, except for Paul? Indeed, since Paul alone among them put on the Baptism of Christ, either the verdict on the danger facing the rest, who lack Christ's water, must be prejudged so the rule stands, or the rule itself must be scrapped if salvation is also established for the unbaptized. I have heard such arguments, with the Lord as my witness, so no one may think me so lost as to stir them up voluntarily out of a lust for writing that only sows scruples in others. And now I will answer, as best I can, those who deny the Apostles were baptized.

If the Apostles had undergone the human baptism of John and desired the Lord's baptism, since the Lord Himself had defined there is only one Baptism, saying to Peter when he refused to be washed: "He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again"—a statement He would never have made to someone who had never been baptized at all—then that is the evident proof against those who strip the Apostles even of John's Baptism, just to destroy the sacrament of water. Can it be believed that the way of the Lord was then being prepared in those persons, that is, the Baptism of John, who were destined to open the way of the Lord throughout the whole world? The Lord Himself, who owed no debt of repentance, was baptized; was it not necessary for sinners? So what? Were the others not baptized? But they were not Christ's companions; they were rivals of the faith, teachers of the law, and Pharisees. From this it is also suggested that, when those who opposed the Lord refused to be baptized, those who followed the Lord were baptized, and did not share the taste of their rivals—especially when the Lord to whom they clung extolled John in testimony, saying: "No one is greater among those born of women than John the Baptist."

Others forcibly argue that the Apostles then fulfilled the role of Baptism when they were sprinkled and covered by waves in the boat, and that Peter himself was sufficiently immersed when he walked on the sea. In my opinion, however, it is one thing to be sprinkled or overwhelmed by the violence of the sea, and another to be baptized by the discipline of religion. Moreover, that boat represented the figure of the Church, which is tossed in the sea—that is, the world—by waves—that is, persecutions and temptations—while the Lord sleeps, as it were, in patience, until He is roused by the prayers of the Saints in the last days, restrains the world, and grants tranquility to His own. Now, whether the Apostles were baptized in some way or remained unbaptized, and whether the Lord's saying about one washing, spoken through Peter's person, applies only to us, it is still far too reckless to speculate on the Apostles' salvation. For them, the privilege of the first calling, and from then on of intimate familiarity, could confer the compendium of Baptism. They followed the One who promised salvation to every believer: "Your faith has saved you," He said, and "Your sins are forgiven"—certainly to the believer, not to the baptized. If that was lacking to the Apostles, I do not know what faith they possessed; with a single word of the Lord, the tax collector rose and abandoned his post; he deserted his father, his boat, and the trade by which he sustained his life; he disregarded his father's funeral: he fulfilled that supreme commandment of the Lord—"Whoever prefers father or mother to me is not worthy of me"—before he had even heard it.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves all clauses and nuances. Pass B provides the required scripture citations (John 3:5) for the alluded verses and maintains the theological distinctions regarding the Apostles' salvation and the nature of the 'tax collector' (Matthew) as the example of faith. All scripture references in the English text match the Latin allusions.
